title: Discernment and standing behind it
header_line: My analysis of one book on an entrepreneur's life. Not a summary of the book. Not affiliated with or endorsed by the author or publisher.

lines.text: How do you learn to tell what is real?
A student asked: how else do you develop discernment other than by being fooled a couple of times?
Another said he goes into situations guardedly optimistic: looking for it to be right, but weighing whether it is real, and putting the weight on himself, not on someone to protect him.
I answered, still arguing the other side, that this is a kind of privilege: the exposure of where you grew up and what you have access to. Not money or education, but exposure.
A student said: if you were the one making the decision, you would feel responsible when it goes wrong. Any human with emotions would.

Another said: I try to look at the overall net positive, even if it means short-term negative. In meetings it is better to take accountability, even if it is painful, because it has a long-term ripple effect on culture.
Another said: say what you want, but you have to stand on it when you say it.
What is a call you would have to stand behind, even if it cost you in the short term?

exercise.title: Five minutes
steps: Write a time you were fooled and what you learned.
Write how you check whether something is real.
Write what exposure helped you most.
Write a call you made for the long term.
Write one thing you will stand behind.

check.q: What did a student ask how else you develop discernment than by?
choices: Being fooled a couple of times

check.q: What did a student say about taking accountability?
choices: It has a long-term ripple effect on culture

check.q: What did I say about exposure?
choices: It is a kind of privilege

recap: Learn discernment by checking. Take accountability. Stand behind what you say.
